title: Complete Project Management Professional Certificate
description: A full 20-module program from beginner to project management professional: initiation, planning, scope/time/cost/quality/risk, communication & stakeholders, leadership, Agile & Scrum, monitoring & control, closure, PM software, business analysis, professional & career skills, 8 practical projects, a capstone and a Certificate of Completion. Prepares you for CAPM®/PMP®.
outcomes: Initiate, plan, execute, monitor & control, and close projects
Build charters, WBS, schedules (Gantt/CPM), budgets and risk registers
Manage scope, time, cost, quality and risk using proven techniques
Communicate with stakeholders and lead high-performing teams
Apply Agile & Scrum and use PM software (MS Project, Jira, Trello, Asana)
Prepare for CAPM®/PMP® and build a project management portfolio
about: This is the complete TIH Project Management Professional Certificate, rebuilt into twenty modules that take you from the basics to professional-level practice.

Every content lesson has a video and printable notes; downloadable templates cover the Project Charter, WBS, Gantt chart, Risk Register, Budget, Status Report, Meeting Minutes and Closure Report, and eight practical projects plus a capstone build your portfolio.

Software & tools: Microsoft Project, Trello, Asana, Jira, Monday.com, ClickUp, Notion, Smartsheet, Excel and Google Workspace. You finish with a full project plan and — after the graduation assessment — a Certificate of Completion, ready for CAPM®/PMP®.
requirements: No prior experience required — we start from the fundamentals
A device to use PM software and complete templates
Willingness to apply each technique to a real or sample project

faqs.question: Will this prepare me for the PMP certification?
faqs.answer: Yes! This course aligns with PMBOK Guide 7th edition and covers all major PMP exam domains. We recommend additional practice exams after completing the course.

faqs.question: Do I need project management experience?
faqs.answer: No prior PM experience is required. The course builds your knowledge from the ground up. Having any work experience (in any field) provides helpful context.

faqs.question: What industries use project management?
faqs.answer: Every industry: construction, healthcare, NGOs, government, banking, technology, agriculture, and more. Every organization that runs projects needs project managers.

faqs.question: How does this course cover Agile and Scrum?
faqs.answer: Module 3 covers Agile fundamentals and Scrum in depth, including sprints, backlogs, retrospectives, and roles. This prepares you for both traditional PM and modern agile environments.

instructor.name: Dr. Mary Weah
instructor.title: Certified PMP & Organizational Strategy Consultant
instructor.bio: Dr. Mary Weah holds PMP and PRINCE2 certifications with 18 years managing large-scale projects for UN agencies, World Bank programs, and Liberian government ministries. She is TIH's Business & Management curriculum lead.

🧭 Welcome to the Course

This lesson develops Welcome to the Course so you can understand how the certificate develops practical project-delivery competence and professional evidence. It connects professional definitions to documents, decisions, measurements, and a realistic delivery example.

1. Purpose
2. People

Definition

The Complete Project Management Professional Certificate is a structured path from beginner foundations to professional practice across predictive and Agile delivery.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Welcome to the Course

The Complete Project Management Professional Certificate is a structured path from beginner foundations to professional practice across predictive and Agile delivery.

project

temporary work undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result

project manager

the person responsible for integrating work and guiding the team toward approved objectives

deliverable

a verifiable output produced by project work

Detailed explanation

You will build charters, schedules, budgets, risk registers, and a portfolio of practical project plans.

The Complete Project Management Professional Certificate is a structured path from beginner foundations to professional practice across predictive and Agile delivery. In professional practice, this topic must be connected to an approved objective, accountable owner, reliable information, and a clear decision or deliverable. Record assumptions so they can be reviewed when conditions change.

  • A project is temporary work that creates a unique result.
  • Project management integrates people, scope, time, cost, quality, risk, communication, and procurement.
  • Success includes stakeholder value, not only finishing tasks.
  • Professional evidence includes decisions, baselines, approvals, results, and lessons.

Step-by-step application

  1. Purpose: define the need, outcome, boundaries, stakeholders, and decision authority.
  2. People: develop the work, estimates, owners, criteria, assumptions, and dependencies.
  3. Plan: compare evidence with the approved plan and discuss causes rather than hiding variance.
  4. Proof: approve action, update controlled records, communicate effects, and capture learning.

Worked example

A learner plans a six-week digital-skills workshop for 40 young people. The project needs a clear outcome, sponsor, participants, schedule, budget, risks, and evidence of completion.

Management questionComplete professional answer
What result is required?State the measurable outcome, beneficiary, due date, constraints, and acceptance authority.
What evidence is needed?Use an approved plan, current actuals, assumptions, decisions, and stakeholder feedback.
What requires action?Explain the variance or risk, its cause and effect, available options, recommendation, owner, and due date.
How will closure be proved?Obtain acceptance, complete handover, archive records, and document lessons and benefits ownership.

Performance picture

PlannedDeliveredForecast

Interpretation: A chart starts a conversation; it does not explain cause by itself. Confirm data quality, identify the variance, forecast the likely outcome, record the decision, and assign the corrective action.

Recommended measure: Success criteria met, stakeholders accept the result, and lessons are documented.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: creating a document only to satisfy a template. Correction: connect every artifact to a real decision and owner.
  • Mistake: changing work without considering time, cost, quality, resources, and risk. Correction: assess integrated effects before approval.
  • Mistake: reporting status without forecast or action. Correction: explain cause, expected outcome, options, recommendation, and accountability.
  • Mistake: treating stakeholder communication as one-way reporting. Correction: confirm understanding and record feedback or decisions.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a project manager apply Welcome to the Course when a community training project is falling behind?

Answer: Verify actual progress and data quality first. Compare results with the approved scope, schedule, budget, and quality expectations. Identify the root cause and affected stakeholders; update risks and issues; develop realistic options; and analyze each option’s effect on benefits and constraints. Recommend one action to the authorized decision-maker, record the decision, update controlled plans only after approval, assign owners and dates, communicate the effect, and monitor whether the action restores the forecast.

Summary

Welcome to the Course belongs to Course Orientation. A competent project professional can define it, apply it to realistic work, produce the right artifact, interpret evidence, make an ethical recommendation, and communicate ownership and next steps.

Project habit: Every important update should answer: What changed? Why? What is the effect? What decision is needed? Who owns the next action, and by when?

This lesson develops Creating Scope Statements so you can define what the project will and will not deliver, control requirements, prevent uncontrolled expansion, and obtain acceptance. It connects professional definitions to documents, decisions, measurements, and a realistic delivery example.

Project delivery model
🎯 Creating Scope Statements
1. Elicit
2. Define
3. Decompose
4. Control
Outcome • owner • baseline • evidence

Definition

A scope statement documents deliverables, acceptance criteria, constraints, and assumptions at a usable level of detail.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Creating Scope Statements

A scope statement documents deliverables, acceptance criteria, constraints, and assumptions at a usable level of detail.

requirement

a documented need or condition that a product, service, or result must satisfy

work breakdown structure

a hierarchical decomposition of project deliverables and work

scope creep

uncontrolled expansion of scope without corresponding approval, resources, time, or budget

Detailed explanation

It is a baseline input once approved.

A scope statement documents deliverables, acceptance criteria, constraints, and assumptions at a usable level of detail. In professional practice, this topic must be connected to an approved objective, accountable owner, reliable information, and a clear decision or deliverable. Record assumptions so they can be reviewed when conditions change.

  • Requirements describe stakeholder needs and conditions a deliverable must meet.
  • A scope statement documents deliverables, boundaries, assumptions, constraints, and acceptance criteria.
  • A WBS decomposes deliverables into manageable work packages.
  • Scope validation accepts completed deliverables; scope control manages baseline changes.

Step-by-step application

  1. Elicit: define the need, outcome, boundaries, stakeholders, and decision authority.
  2. Define: develop the work, estimates, owners, criteria, assumptions, and dependencies.
  3. Decompose: compare evidence with the approved plan and discuss causes rather than hiding variance.
  4. Control: approve action, update controlled records, communicate effects, and capture learning.

Worked example

For a website project, stakeholders agree required pages, mobile behavior, content responsibilities, acceptance tests, exclusions, and a process for evaluating requested additions.

Management questionComplete professional answer
What result is required?State the measurable outcome, beneficiary, due date, constraints, and acceptance authority.
What evidence is needed?Use an approved plan, current actuals, assumptions, decisions, and stakeholder feedback.
What requires action?Explain the variance or risk, its cause and effect, available options, recommendation, owner, and due date.
How will closure be proved?Obtain acceptance, complete handover, archive records, and document lessons and benefits ownership.

Performance picture

PlannedDeliveredForecast

Interpretation: A chart starts a conversation; it does not explain cause by itself. Confirm data quality, identify the variance, forecast the likely outcome, record the decision, and assign the corrective action.

Recommended measure: Every deliverable traces to an approved requirement and has clear acceptance evidence.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: creating a document only to satisfy a template. Correction: connect every artifact to a real decision and owner.
  • Mistake: changing work without considering time, cost, quality, resources, and risk. Correction: assess integrated effects before approval.
  • Mistake: reporting status without forecast or action. Correction: explain cause, expected outcome, options, recommendation, and accountability.
  • Mistake: treating stakeholder communication as one-way reporting. Correction: confirm understanding and record feedback or decisions.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a project manager apply Creating Scope Statements when a community training project is falling behind?

Answer: Verify actual progress and data quality first. Compare results with the approved scope, schedule, budget, and quality expectations. Identify the root cause and affected stakeholders; update risks and issues; develop realistic options; and analyze each option’s effect on benefits and constraints. Recommend one action to the authorized decision-maker, record the decision, update controlled plans only after approval, assign owners and dates, communicate the effect, and monitor whether the action restores the forecast.

Summary

Creating Scope Statements belongs to Project Scope Management. A competent project professional can define it, apply it to realistic work, produce the right artifact, interpret evidence, make an ethical recommendation, and communicate ownership and next steps.

Project habit: Every important update should answer: What changed? Why? What is the effect? What decision is needed? Who owns the next action, and by when?

Definition

Activity definition identifies the specific schedule activities required to produce WBS work packages.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Activity Definition

Activity definition identifies the specific schedule activities required to produce WBS work packages.

milestone

a significant zero-duration point marking an event, decision, or achievement

a logical relationship that determines the order in which activities occur

the longest-duration network path that determines the project’s earliest finish date

Activities are actionable; work packages are deliverable-oriented.

Project delivery model
📈 Issue Tracking
1. Measure
2. Compare
3. Forecast
4. Act
Outcome • owner • baseline • evidence

Definition

Issue tracking logs problems that need resolution, with owners, priority, and due dates.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Issue Tracking

Issue tracking logs problems that need resolution, with owners, priority, and due dates.

earned value

the budgeted value of work actually completed

schedule performance index

earned value divided by planned value; below 1.0 indicates less work completed than planned

change control

the formal process for evaluating, approving, rejecting, recording, and communicating changes

Detailed explanation

Separate issues (happening now) from risks (uncertain future).

Issue tracking logs problems that need resolution, with owners, priority, and due dates. In professional practice, this topic must be connected to an approved objective, accountable owner, reliable information, and a clear decision or deliverable. Record assumptions so they can be reviewed when conditions change.

  • Monitoring collects and interprets performance information; control takes approved action.
  • Variance describes a difference from plan; trend analysis shows direction over time.
  • Integrated change control assesses effects before changing baselines.
  • Status reports should explain meaning, forecast, decisions, and ownership—not only color labels.

Step-by-step application

  1. Measure: define the need, outcome, boundaries, stakeholders, and decision authority.
  2. Compare: develop the work, estimates, owners, criteria, assumptions, and dependencies.
  3. Forecast: compare evidence with the approved plan and discuss causes rather than hiding variance.
  4. Act: approve action, update controlled records, communicate effects, and capture learning.

Worked example

At the monthly review, a project reports completed work, spending, milestones, risks, issues, changes, and forecasts. The steering group approves corrective action based on evidence.

Management questionComplete professional answer
What result is required?State the measurable outcome, beneficiary, due date, constraints, and acceptance authority.
What evidence is needed?Use an approved plan, current actuals, assumptions, decisions, and stakeholder feedback.
What requires action?Explain the variance or risk, its cause and effect, available options, recommendation, owner, and due date.
How will closure be proved?Obtain acceptance, complete handover, archive records, and document lessons and benefits ownership.

Performance picture

PlannedDeliveredForecast

Interpretation: A chart starts a conversation; it does not explain cause by itself. Confirm data quality, identify the variance, forecast the likely outcome, record the decision, and assign the corrective action.

Recommended measure: Use SV = EV − PV, CV = EV − AC, SPI = EV ÷ PV, CPI = EV ÷ AC, plus milestone and risk trends.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: creating a document only to satisfy a template. Correction: connect every artifact to a real decision and owner.
  • Mistake: changing work without considering time, cost, quality, resources, and risk. Correction: assess integrated effects before approval.
  • Mistake: reporting status without forecast or action. Correction: explain cause, expected outcome, options, recommendation, and accountability.
  • Mistake: treating stakeholder communication as one-way reporting. Correction: confirm understanding and record feedback or decisions.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a project manager apply Issue Tracking when a community training project is falling behind?

Answer: Verify actual progress and data quality first. Compare results with the approved scope, schedule, budget, and quality expectations. Identify the root cause and affected stakeholders; update risks and issues; develop realistic options; and analyze each option’s effect on benefits and constraints. Recommend one action to the authorized decision-maker, record the decision, update controlled plans only after approval, assign owners and dates, communicate the effect, and monitor whether the action restores the forecast.

Summary

Issue Tracking belongs to Project Monitoring & Control. A competent project professional can define it, apply it to realistic work, produce the right artifact, interpret evidence, make an ethical recommendation, and communicate ownership and next steps.

Project habit: Every important update should answer: What changed? Why? What is the effect? What decision is needed? Who owns the next action, and by when?

Module 17: Professional SkillsComplete lesson

🌟 Proposal Writing

This lesson develops Proposal Writing so you can communicate clearly, negotiate ethically, think critically, make evidence-based decisions, solve problems, and manage personal effectiveness. It connects professional definitions to documents, decisions, measurements, and a realistic delivery example.

Project delivery model
🌟 Proposal Writing
1. Listen
2. Analyze
3. Decide
4. Communicate
Outcome • owner • baseline • evidence

Definition

Proposal writing presents an approach, scope, timeline, and price to win or approve work.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Proposal Writing

Proposal writing presents an approach, scope, timeline, and price to win or approve work.

critical thinking

disciplined evaluation of evidence, assumptions, logic, and alternatives

negotiation

a structured process for reaching agreement while managing interests and relationships

decision log

a record of important decisions, rationale, owner, date, and resulting actions

Detailed explanation

Mirror the client’s problem language.

Proposal writing presents an approach, scope, timeline, and price to win or approve work. In professional practice, this topic must be connected to an approved objective, accountable owner, reliable information, and a clear decision or deliverable. Record assumptions so they can be reviewed when conditions change.

  • Professional judgment separates facts, assumptions, constraints, and preferences.
  • Negotiation focuses on interests and options rather than only positions.
  • Decisions should state criteria, owner, timing, rationale, and consequences.
  • Time and stress management protect both performance and relationships.

Step-by-step application

  1. Listen: define the need, outcome, boundaries, stakeholders, and decision authority.
  2. Analyze: develop the work, estimates, owners, criteria, assumptions, and dependencies.
  3. Decide: compare evidence with the approved plan and discuss causes rather than hiding variance.
  4. Communicate: approve action, update controlled records, communicate effects, and capture learning.

Worked example

A supplier delay threatens a public event. The project manager gathers facts, identifies options, negotiates alternatives, records the decision, communicates impact, and follows up.

Management questionComplete professional answer
What result is required?State the measurable outcome, beneficiary, due date, constraints, and acceptance authority.
What evidence is needed?Use an approved plan, current actuals, assumptions, decisions, and stakeholder feedback.
What requires action?Explain the variance or risk, its cause and effect, available options, recommendation, owner, and due date.
How will closure be proved?Obtain acceptance, complete handover, archive records, and document lessons and benefits ownership.

Performance picture

PlannedDeliveredForecast

Interpretation: A chart starts a conversation; it does not explain cause by itself. Confirm data quality, identify the variance, forecast the likely outcome, record the decision, and assign the corrective action.

Recommended measure: Review decision quality, follow-through, communication clarity, relationship health, and learning.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: creating a document only to satisfy a template. Correction: connect every artifact to a real decision and owner.
  • Mistake: changing work without considering time, cost, quality, resources, and risk. Correction: assess integrated effects before approval.
  • Mistake: reporting status without forecast or action. Correction: explain cause, expected outcome, options, recommendation, and accountability.
  • Mistake: treating stakeholder communication as one-way reporting. Correction: confirm understanding and record feedback or decisions.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a project manager apply Proposal Writing when a community training project is falling behind?

Answer: Verify actual progress and data quality first. Compare results with the approved scope, schedule, budget, and quality expectations. Identify the root cause and affected stakeholders; update risks and issues; develop realistic options; and analyze each option’s effect on benefits and constraints. Recommend one action to the authorized decision-maker, record the decision, update controlled plans only after approval, assign owners and dates, communicate the effect, and monitor whether the action restores the forecast.

Summary

Proposal Writing belongs to Professional Skills. A competent project professional can define it, apply it to realistic work, produce the right artifact, interpret evidence, make an ethical recommendation, and communicate ownership and next steps.

Project habit: Every important update should answer: What changed? Why? What is the effect? What decision is needed? Who owns the next action, and by when?

lessons.title: 18.8 Career Growth Roadmap
lessons.html:
Module 18: Career DevelopmentComplete lesson

💼 Career Growth Roadmap

This lesson develops Career Growth Roadmap so you can turn project-management knowledge into a credible portfolio, focused résumé, interview evidence, certification plan, and career roadmap. It connects professional definitions to documents, decisions, measurements, and a realistic delivery example.

Project delivery model
💼 Career Growth Roadmap
1. Target
2. Build
3. Evidence
4. Present
Outcome • owner • baseline • evidence

Definition

A career growth roadmap sequences skills, certifications, domain depth, and leadership scope over years.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Career Growth Roadmap

A career growth roadmap sequences skills, certifications, domain depth, and leadership scope over years.

portfolio

a curated set of project artifacts and explanations demonstrating competence

STAR method

an interview structure covering situation, task, action, and result

competency

an observable combination of knowledge, skill, behavior, and judgment

Detailed explanation

Pick an industry lane to deepen value.

A career growth roadmap sequences skills, certifications, domain depth, and leadership scope over years. In professional practice, this topic must be connected to an approved objective, accountable owner, reliable information, and a clear decision or deliverable. Record assumptions so they can be reviewed when conditions change.

  • A portfolio should show decisions, artifacts, outcomes, and reflection.
  • Résumé statements are stronger when they name action, context, and measurable result.
  • Interview answers should use specific evidence rather than unsupported claims.
  • Certification requirements, costs, experience rules, and renewal obligations must be verified.

Step-by-step application

  1. Target: define the need, outcome, boundaries, stakeholders, and decision authority.
  2. Build: develop the work, estimates, owners, criteria, assumptions, and dependencies.
  3. Evidence: compare evidence with the approved plan and discuss causes rather than hiding variance.
  4. Present: approve action, update controlled records, communicate effects, and capture learning.

Worked example

A learner selects a coordinator role, maps required competencies, completes a community-project portfolio, writes achievement statements, practices STAR answers, and verifies certification eligibility.

Management questionComplete professional answer
What result is required?State the measurable outcome, beneficiary, due date, constraints, and acceptance authority.
What evidence is needed?Use an approved plan, current actuals, assumptions, decisions, and stakeholder feedback.
What requires action?Explain the variance or risk, its cause and effect, available options, recommendation, owner, and due date.
How will closure be proved?Obtain acceptance, complete handover, archive records, and document lessons and benefits ownership.

Performance picture

PlannedDeliveredForecast

Interpretation: A chart starts a conversation; it does not explain cause by itself. Confirm data quality, identify the variance, forecast the likely outcome, record the decision, and assign the corrective action.

Recommended measure: Track role readiness, evidence gaps, applications, interviews, feedback, professional connections, and learning milestones.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Mistake: creating a document only to satisfy a template. Correction: connect every artifact to a real decision and owner.
  • Mistake: changing work without considering time, cost, quality, resources, and risk. Correction: assess integrated effects before approval.
  • Mistake: reporting status without forecast or action. Correction: explain cause, expected outcome, options, recommendation, and accountability.
  • Mistake: treating stakeholder communication as one-way reporting. Correction: confirm understanding and record feedback or decisions.

Guided practice with detailed answer

Question: How should a project manager apply Career Growth Roadmap when a community training project is falling behind?

Answer: Verify actual progress and data quality first. Compare results with the approved scope, schedule, budget, and quality expectations. Identify the root cause and affected stakeholders; update risks and issues; develop realistic options; and analyze each option’s effect on benefits and constraints. Recommend one action to the authorized decision-maker, record the decision, update controlled plans only after approval, assign owners and dates, communicate the effect, and monitor whether the action restores the forecast.

Summary

Career Growth Roadmap belongs to Career Development. A competent project professional can define it, apply it to realistic work, produce the right artifact, interpret evidence, make an ethical recommendation, and communicate ownership and next steps.

Project habit: Every important update should answer: What changed? Why? What is the effect? What decision is needed? Who owns the next action, and by when?

lessons.title: 20.1 Certificate Requirements
lessons.html:
Module 20: Assessments & GraduationGraduation

Certificate Requirements

To graduate and earn your TIH Certificate of Completion you must:

  • Complete the lessons in Modules 1–18.
  • Complete the practical projects in Module 19 (incl. a Complete Project Management Plan).
  • Deliver the Capstone Project Presentation and pass the Portfolio Review.
  • Pass the skill assessments, the Midterm and Final Examinations.
  • Pass the final Certificate of Completion assessment.
